name: Licochalcone A
lead: Licochalcone A is a chalcone-type phenol isolated from the roots of licorice species (Glycyrrhiza inflata and G. glabra) [1][2]. In skincare it appears in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin and is also discussed for its possible effect on pigment production [4].

Laboratory research has reported antioxidant, antibacterial, antimalarial and anticancer activity [1][5][6][7], and licorice flavonoids have been examined for tyrosinase inhibition [4]. Human data on appearance come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so the contribution of licochalcone A alone cannot be separated [8][9].

paras: Six licorice flavonoids including licochalcone A were characterised in a 2013 study for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity [2]. A 1998 study reported superoxide-scavenging and antioxidative activity of retrochalcones from G. inflata [3]. A 2005 study isolated licorice flavonoids and tested their inhibitory effect on tyrosinase [4]. Other lab work reported activity against Plasmodium falciparum, bacteria and Helicobacter pylori, and against prostate cancer cells [5][6][7][10].

A completed phase 3 trial (n=120) tested a moisturizer containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and 1,2-decanediol alongside adapalene gel in acne [8]. A completed trial (n=50) tested a moisturizer containing licochalcone A, decanediol, L-carnitine and salicylic acid for reducing acne relapse [9]. Both used multi-ingredient products, and results are not in the sources reviewed. No studies found on licochalcone A alone for pigmentation or redness.

timeline.event: Licochalcone A reported as an antimalarial agent in vitro [5].
Licorice flavonoids examined for tyrosinase inhibition [4].

card.summary: A licorice-root chalcone used in soothing skincare, with lab hints of tyrosinase inhibition and only combination-product acne trials in humans.
card.note: Human data are multi-ingredient acne products; pigment and redness claims rest on lab work.

quick.overview:
Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root that shows up in sensitive-skin and acne-care products. It is also discussed for possible brightening effects.

Human studies found were acne trials of moisturizers containing several actives, so its own effect cannot be isolated.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work reports antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed give no skin safety data. Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, relevant to handling rather than finished products.
